summary: This experimental RFC describes a home agent-assisted route optimization for IPv4 Network Mobility. It is meant for cases where all nodes use a single home agent, such as within one organization. It enables discovery of eligible peer nodes and lets traffic take a more direct path.

eli5.summary: When a moving network sends a message to a friend in the same group, it does not have to go the long way round. This helps them find each other and take a shortcut.

questions: what is home agent assisted route optimization
how do mobile routers discover each other
what is the return routability procedure
subtitle: Direct routing between mobile networks through a shared home agent

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv4 networks that all use the same home agent normally route all traffic through that home agent, causing bottlenecks and delays. Sites that belong to the same organization cannot take more direct paths.
tldr.mechanism: Mobile routers discover each other's networks through the home agent, establish secure bindings using a return routability check, and create direct tunnels to bypass the home agent for traffic between known peers.
tldr.outcome: Traffic between mobile networks flows directly rather than through a centralized home agent, reducing latency and load. This works only within a single administrative domain sharing one home agent.

facts.label: Use case
facts.value: Mobile networks in single organization sharing one home agent

today: RFC 6521 remains Experimental and has not been moved to Standards Track. It addresses a specific scenario (multiple mobile networks under one organization and home agent) but has seen limited deployment. The procedures remain viable for enterprise networks that choose to implement this optimization.

sections.title: Mobile IPv4 Route Optimization
sections.content:
Mobile IPv4 lets networks stay connected as they move between Internet service providers. But it does this by routing all traffic through a home agent: a fixed router that acts as a post office, forwarding packets to wherever the network has moved. This creates a problem for enterprise networks with multiple sites all managed by the same home agent—every message between sites, even those physically close together, takes a long detour through the home agent.

RFC 6521 solves this for a specific but practical case: when all mobile routers in an organization connect to the same home agent. It lets them discover each other and set up direct paths between their networks, so traffic no longer needs to pass through the central bottleneck.
sections.eli5: All the moving networks in a company used to send mail through one central office. This RFC lets them recognize each other and pass mail directly when they're close together.

sections.title: How Discovery and Registration Work
sections.content:
The core idea is that the home agent already knows which networks are managed by each mobile router. Instead of keeping this information secret, the home agent shares it with the other routers as part of the registration process. When router A registers, it learns that router B exists and manages network B. When router B registers, it learns about both router A and router C.

To keep the amount of data manageable, especially with hundreds of networks, the RFC includes two compression schemes: one for network prefixes (which often differ only slightly from each other) and one for realms, which identify administrative domains like 'example.org' or 'branch-office.example.com'.
sections.eli5: When each moving network checks in with the home agent, the home agent tells it about all the other networks so they can find each other.

sections.title: Return Routability and Tunnel Setup
sections.content:
Before two mobile routers can trust each other, they perform a return routability check. Router A sends two test messages to router B: one through the home agent (to verify that router B's home address is real) and one directly from router A's current location (to prove router A can send from that location). Router B responds with both a home keygen token and a care-of keygen token. These tokens, combined with shared secrets in router A, create a registration key that lets both routers authenticate each other.

Once the return routability check completes, router A can send a Registration Request directly to router B. If router B already knows about router A's networks from the home agent advertisement, it accepts the request. Both routers then establish a direct tunnel between their current locations. Packets travel through this tunnel encapsulated in UDP or IP-in-IP, depending on what the network allows.
sections.eli5: Before trusting each other, two routers exchange secret messages: one the long way (through the home agent) and one the direct way. If both messages get through, they know they can send mail to each other directly.

sections.title: The Route Optimization Cache
sections.content:
Each mobile router maintains a Route Optimization Cache with information about every peer it can optimize to. For each peer, the router tracks the peer's home address, its current care-of addresses, the status of the return routability check (INACTIVE, IN PROGRESS, or ACTIVE), the network prefixes the peer manages, the tunnel interface to use, and whether NAT is involved.

The cache is built up over time. The home agent provides initial information when the router registers. Additional entries are added when the router receives Registration Requests from other routers for the first time, or when it proactively discovers new peers. Entries can be dropped if memory is tight or if they become stale.
sections.eli5: Each router keeps a notebook of other routers it knows about: their addresses, which networks they run, whether the tunnel to them is working, and whether they've passed the trust test.

sections.title: Handovers and Topology Changes
sections.content:
When a mobile router moves to a new ISP and gets a new care-of address, it sends an updated Registration Request to its home agent. It also sends updates to any peer routers it has active tunnels with, and it may need to redo part of the return routability check with a new care-of keygen token. During a handover, the router keeps accepting packets from both the old and new locations for a grace period to avoid losing in-flight packets.

If a mobile router completely leaves the network (joining its home link), it sends deregistration requests with lifetime zero to both the home agent and all peer routers. The peers then remove the router's network prefixes from their Route Optimization Caches and routing tables, causing traffic to fall back to going through the home agent.
sections.eli5: When a network moves to a new ISP, it tells its peers about its new location. Until everyone gets the message, they might try both the old and new locations. When it goes back home, it tells everyone to stop using the direct tunnel.

sections.title: Trust and Security
sections.content:
The scheme relies on two trust relationships: First, all mobile routers trust the home agent. The home agent tells them which networks are managed by which routers, and the routers take this information at face value. Second, two routers trust each other once they've completed the return routability check; this proves that the home address is reachable at that location.

However, a router claiming to represent a specific network prefix is not automatically trusted. If router A receives a Registration Request from router B claiming to manage network B, router A can verify this by checking whether the home agent's earlier advertisement listed network B as managed by router B. Only if the information matches, or if the environment is configured as trusted, should the registration be accepted.
sections.eli5: All routers trust what the home agent tells them. When two routers talk directly, they prove they're really who they say they are. But if a router claims to run a network, the other router checks with the home agent to make sure that's true.
